01

What is AI, really?

Not magic. Not a brain. A pattern-finder.

Ask the room first: "Finish this sentence: AI is…" Take 3 answers (you'll hear "a robot", "a brain", "ChatGPT"). "Let's replace all of those with what it actually is."

The big idea

Rules vs. examples.

1

Normal code: a person writes the rules

“If the subject says FREE PRIZE, it's spam.” Spell it FR3E and it slips through.

2

AI: show it examples instead

10,000 emails labeled spam or not spam. It works out the pattern on its own.

3

That's machine learning

Software whose behavior was learned from data, not typed in line by line.

AI learns its rules from examples.

~2 min. The laptop acts it out: on the left, rules a person wrote. A sneaky email ("FR3E PR1ZE") gets past because no rule matches. On the right, a filter that learned from thousands of labeled emails catches it, even though nobody wrote a rule about weird spelling. Click 1: normal code. Every rule is typed by a human. Humans can't think of every trick. Click 2: machine learning. You don't write rules; you collect examples with the right answers (labels). Click 3: that's the definition. Everything we call "AI" today is built this way. Ask: "What's one job you'd rather teach with examples than with rules?" (recognizing your friend's face, knowing a song is sad, spotting a cat). Those are hard to write as rules, easy to show with examples.

Training vs. using

Learn once. Use it a billion times.

1

Read

Trillions of words: websites, books, code.

2

Practice for months

Hide the next word, guess it, check it. Patterns form.

3

Freeze it, then use it

Every chat after that is called inference: prediction only.

It predicts what sounds right — not what is right.

~2 min. One click per step. The model on the right follows you: pages pile up (read), spread into a web of connections (patterns), then collapse into a phone's next-word strip (predict). Two vocabulary words to leave with: - TRAINING: the expensive part. Months, thousands of special chips (GPUs), huge electricity bills. Done once. - INFERENCE: using the finished model. Your message in, a prediction out, in seconds. Important: after training, the model does NOT keep learning from your chat. That's why it has a "knowledge cutoff": it doesn't know what happened after its training data was collected. Last click is the most important sentence of today: "It predicts what SOUNDS right, not what IS right." Have the room say it back. We'll prove it in the ethics section.

What's inside a model

Billions of tiny dials.

1

Parameters

A model is a giant list of numbers. Each one is a dial, also called a weight.

2

Wrong guess? Nudge the dials.

Each mistake nudges every dial a tiny bit toward the right answer.

3

More dials, more patterns

GPT-2 (2019): 1.5 billion. GPT-3 (2020): 175 billion. Llama 3.1 (2024): 405 billion.

No one wrote the rules. Training did.

~2 min. The dials on the model: click 1 shows the bank, click 2 they hunt back and forth (guess and check), click 3 they settle (adjusted). Analogy: tuning a guitar with billions of strings at once. You don't know which string is off, so after every wrong note you nudge ALL of them a tiny bit in the direction that would have sounded better. The math that figures out which way to nudge is called gradient descent. You don't need the math; you need the idea: small corrections, repeated billions of times. The numbers on click 3 are public: GPT-2 and GPT-3 from OpenAI's papers, Llama 3.1 405B from Meta. Many newer companies don't publish their counts anymore. Why it matters: nobody wrote "after 'turned on the', say TV". The pattern was found, not programmed. That's why even the people who build these models can't always explain one specific answer.

02

How does it actually work?

Follow one sentence through the machine.

"Now we open the box. We'll follow one sentence through the five steps an LLM takes every time it writes a single word. This is the stuff we'll build on for the next five weeks." The phone is already doing it: watch it pick words one at a time.

Quick game

Guess the next word.

After school I grabbed a snack and turned on the

Shout it out!

~1 min. Read the sentence out loud and pause. Let people shout guesses. Collect 4–5 answers. Most people say TV, Xbox, music… Nobody says "oven". Why? You've seen thousands of sentences like this, so your brain predicted the next word. An LLM plays this exact game, every single word. "Let's watch the five steps it goes through to make ONE guess."

Step 1 · Tokens

It sees tokens. Not letters.

unbelievable
strawberry

Each chunk becomes an ID number. Every AI cuts words a little differently.

Try it:

How many r's are in “strawberry”?

Too famous? Ask: how many s's are in “Mississippi assessments”?

~2 min. Click once: the words split into tokens (the keycaps split too). "Step one: chop the text into chunks called tokens. A token is often part of a word; roughly 3/4 of a word on average in English. Each token gets an ID number. The model never sees letters, only those numbers." Why it matters: counting letters is weirdly hard for it, and long chats are measured (and priced) in tokens. Click again: the r's light up. Try it live. Heads-up: many newer AIs now get "strawberry" right because the riddle went viral. That's memorizing, not seeing. Use the Mississippi one: the answer is 9 (4 in Mississippi + 5 in assessments).

Step 2 · Embeddings

Tokens become numbers.

1

Each token gets a list of numbers

“dog” → [0.21, −1.40, 0.88, …], often thousands of numbers long.

2

Similar meanings land close together

cat sits near dog. pizza sits near taco. Training put them there.

3

Directions mean things

king − man + woman lands near queen.

To an AI, meaning is where a word sits.

~2 min. The tablet shows a flattened map: real embeddings have hundreds to thousands of dimensions, we squash them to 2D so humans can see. Analogy: every word gets a GPS address in "meaning space". Words used in similar ways get nearby addresses. Click 3: the famous trick. Walk from "man" to "woman" on the map. Take the same walk starting from "king" and you land near "queen". That direction means something like "female version of". (This classic example comes from an older word model, word2vec. Modern LLMs do a fancier version, but the idea holds.) Bridge: these numbers are also how AI search works: find text whose numbers sit near your question's numbers. Also a sneak peek at ethics: if the training text links certain jobs with certain genders, the map does too.

Step 3 · Attention

Words look at each other.

1

Same word, different meaning

“river bank” vs. “bank account.” The word alone can't tell you which.

2

Every word scores every other word

“How much should you change what I mean?” Big score, big influence.

3

Stacked dozens of layers deep

This is the transformer, the “T” in GPT. Invented in 2017.

Context changes the meaning.

~2 min. The laptop: two sentences take turns. Watch how "bank" pays most attention to "river" in the first and to "money" in the second, then its meaning updates. Click 2: every word does this with every other word at the same time, and the scores add up to 100%. The word's numbers (its spot on the meaning map) get updated toward the words it paid attention to. Click 3: one round of attention is a "layer". Big models stack dozens to over a hundred layers, so meaning gets refined again and again: by the top, "bank" knows it's a riverbank in a story about fishing. GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The 2017 Google paper was called "Attention Is All You Need". This is also why the context window matters (coming up): attention can only look at what's on the page.

Step 4 · Score every option

Every word gets a score.

TV41%
Xbox22%
music15%
lights12%
PlayStation7%
oven1%

Every token in its vocabulary gets a score.

Numbers are made up to show the idea.

~1 min. Click once: bars grow. "After the attention layers, the model looks at the last position and gives EVERY token it knows a score. A typical vocabulary is 50,000 to 200,000 tokens, so that's a lot of scores. They're turned into probabilities that add up to 100%. Those are the bars." The wheel on the right is the same idea in motion: likelier words own more of the wheel, so it usually lands on TV, and now and then it doesn't. That "now and then" is the next step.

Step 5 · Pick one, then repeat

Same question. Different answer.

1

It doesn't always pick #1

A setting called temperature adds randomness. Low = safe and samey. High = creative and weird.

2

Two answers disagree? At least one is wrong.

If they agree, still check. Agreeing isn't proof.

Add the word. Repeat. That's everything.

~2 min, live. Open two NEW chats on the projector and ask both: "Give my band a name." The room sees two different answers (the phones on the slide do the same). Click 1: why. It samples from the scores with a bit of randomness (temperature). Temperature 0 picks the top word almost every time; higher temperatures pick unlikely words more often. Click 2: useful trick. Ask both chats a fact question you already checked. Different answers = red flag. Click 3: the full loop. Pick a token, add it to the text, run ALL five steps again for the next token. An essay of 500 words is this loop running roughly 650 times. Recap the five steps out loud: tokens → embeddings → attention → scores → pick. Then repeat.

The context window

It only knows what's on the page.

1

The page is this chat

Everything you typed and everything it answered, measured in tokens.

2

New chat, blank page

The model doesn't remember you. Apps with “memory” paste saved notes in for you.

3

Long chat, fuzzy start

Once the page is full, the oldest parts fall off or get blurry.

If it needs to know it, put it on the page.

~2 min. The model on the right: a long conversation, and a frame showing the part the AI can use. "When it answers it has exactly two things: the frozen patterns from training (the dials), and the text in front of it right now. That text is the context window." Click 1: context windows are measured in tokens. Today's big models handle hundreds of thousands, some a million+. Click 2: memory features are the app writing notes about you and quietly pasting them into the page. Click 3: in very long chats, early rules get lost. Say the important rule again. Building tip: when your code breaks, paste the code AND the error message. It can't see your screen.

03

LLMs vs. the rest of AI

One family. Many different jobs.

"Everything we just learned is how ONE kind of AI works: a large language model. Most of the AI you touch every day is not an LLM. Let's sort them out."

The AI family tree

Where LLMs fit.

1

Artificial intelligence

Any computer doing something that seems smart. Even 1997's chess champion, Deep Blue.

2

Machine learning

AI that learns from examples instead of hand-written rules.

3

Deep learning

Machine learning with many stacked layers: a neural network.

4

Generative AI → LLMs

Deep learning that makes new things. LLMs make text: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude.

~1.5 min. The tablet lights up each ring, outside in, with examples. Each ring sits inside the one before it. Every LLM is generative AI, which is deep learning, which is machine learning, which is AI. But not the other way around. Deep Blue (IBM, beat world champion Kasparov in 1997) is AI but mostly NOT machine learning: it searched millions of chess moves using rules and scoring that people wrote. Good example of "AI ≠ learning". "LLM" = Large (billions of parameters, trillions of training tokens) Language (trained on text) Model (the frozen pile of dials). Many are now "multimodal": they also take images and audio.

You probably used all four today

Four jobs AI does.

1

Recommend

Your For You feed, YouTube, Spotify. Learns from what you watch and skip.

2

Recognize

Face ID, spam filters, photo search. Sorts what it sees into labels.

3

Create images

Image generators. Different machine from an LLM (next slide).

4

Create text

LLMs. Predict the next token, over and over.

~1.5 min. Hands up after each one: "Who used this today?" (Almost everyone, for 1 and 2.) The phones: a feed telling you WHY it picked a video, and a face unlock recognizing a face. 1 Recommend: predicts how likely YOU are to watch, like, or finish something. Every swipe is training data. 2 Recognize (classify): input → a label. Face → "owner / not owner". Email → "spam / not spam". 3 & 4 Generate: make something new. Key point: same core idea (learn patterns from examples), very different jobs and training data. A recommender is not an LLM and can't chat. An LLM isn't built to recommend your next video.

Not every AI is an LLM

Image AIs paint from static.

1

Start with pure noise

Random colored dots, like old TV static.

2

Remove a little noise, many times

Each step it guesses what the picture should look like, steered by your prompt.

3

Trained on captioned images

Millions of pictures with descriptions. It learns patterns, and sometimes memorizes.

Text AI: next token. Image AI: less noise.

~1.5 min. The laptop runs a pretend generation: static → blocky shapes → a fox in the snow. This is called a DIFFUSION model (Stable Diffusion, Midjourney and many others work roughly this way). Say "most image AIs": some newer ones, like the image generator inside ChatGPT, use a different method. How it was trained: take a real photo, add noise to it, and teach the model to predict the noise you added. Do that millions of times. Then at generation time, start from pure noise and keep removing predicted noise, nudged toward the prompt. Contrast with an LLM: an LLM builds text left to right, one token at a time. A diffusion model refines the WHOLE image at once, a little better each step. Click 3 plants a seed for ethics: those training images came from real artists and photographers.

04

Model. Chatbot. Agent.

Three words people mix up. First, watch one.

Hand off to the adult sponsor for the live demo. "We'll watch an AI agent build something, then take apart what we saw: what's the model, what's the chatbot, what's the agent."

Live demo · an AI agent (Claude Code)

One prompt. Watch it build.

> claude Build a one-page website for our teen AI workshop. Include a countdown to demo day, the list of 6 sessions, and a button that shows a random fun fact about AI. Then publish it on GitHub Pages.

Your job:

Call out changes!

“Dark mode.”

“Add confetti.”

“Make it purple.”

~3 min (keep it tight). ADULT SPONSOR runs this live from their own Claude account on the projector. (Claude is 18+, so the teens don't log in to Claude themselves. Say this out loud.) 1. Type the prompt shown. Narrate what it's doing: planning, creating files, running commands. 2. Open the first working page locally. Take ONE change request from the room and make it. 3. Don't wait for a live deploy (that alone takes 1–2 minutes). Switch to a copy you published beforehand, so the room still sees a real URL. Use a clean folder and a demo account: no tokens, emails or other projects visible in the terminal. Point out the moments it RUNS something and READS the result. That's the difference we're about to name. If Wi-Fi fails: play the backup recording.

What just happened?

An AI agent works in a loop.

Plan Write code Fix what broke Run it
~1 min. "A chatbot answers once and waits for you. An agent keeps going on its own: plans, writes code, runs it, reads what broke, fixes it, repeats until the job is done. That's why it could build a whole site." Under the hood it's the same next-token model. The difference is what's wrapped around it. Next two slides. "You'll use the same loop when you build, except YOU are the one checking each step."

Model → chatbot

A raw model just keeps typing.

1

Raw (base) model

Ask “How do I bake a cake?” and it may continue: “How do I bake bread? How do I…”

2

Coaching makes it an assistant

Trained on example chats, then people rate answers. Better answers win.

3

An app wraps it

Hidden instructions (the system prompt), safety rules, chat history, a nice screen.

Chatbot = model + coaching + an app.

~2 min. Left side of the tablet: a raw model "answering" by continuing the text, because that's all pre-training taught it: predict what comes next on a web page (and web pages often list more questions). Click 2: two coaching stages. - Instruction tuning: train on thousands of example conversations written by people. - Learning from human feedback (RLHF): show two answers, a person picks the better one, nudge the dials toward answers people prefer. The tablet shows the 👍. This is also where "be helpful, be honest, refuse dangerous stuff" gets taught, and where the habit of sounding confident sneaks in: people tend to rate confident answers higher. Click 3: the app (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude.ai) adds a hidden system prompt you never see, safety filters, and your chat history. Same model, different app = different behavior.

Chatbot → agent

The model guesses. Tools let it act.

1

Search

It can read live web pages, then write from them.

2

Run code

It can test the program or do the math, instead of guessing.

3

See

Photos, screenshots, files.

Model + tools + a loop = an agent.

~1.5 min. One click per tool; each tile appears on the model. How tools work: the model can't touch the internet. It writes a special message like "search: Burch Library hours". The app runs the search, pastes the results back onto the page (the context window!), and the model keeps writing. Same next-token trick, just with fresh text to read. Search: not stuck at its training cutoff. Look for links or a "searched the web" label. Run code: math and data by actually computing. See: show it a screenshot of your broken page. Last click: give it tools AND let it decide its next step on its own, over and over = an agent. Tools make it better, not perfect. It can pick a bad source, misread a good one, or run the wrong command.

Put it together

Model vs. chatbot vs. agent.

MODEL

The engine

DOES

Predicts the next token

REMEMBERS

Only the page it's given

CAN ACT?

No. Text out only.

EXAMPLE

The GPT, Gemini, Claude models

CHATBOT

Engine + an app

DOES

Answers one message at a time

REMEMBERS

Chat history, saved notes

CAN ACT?

Mostly talks. Some search.

EXAMPLE

ChatGPT, the Gemini app

AGENT

Engine + tools + loop

DOES

Works step by step to a goal

REMEMBERS

Files, notes, its own results

CAN ACT?

Runs code, edits files, browses

EXAMPLE

Claude Code, Copilot agent mode

Same engine. More built around it.

~1.5 min. One column per click. Quick quiz after: point at things and ask "model, chatbot, or agent?" - A model name like "GPT" or "Gemini" on its own → model. - The ChatGPT app → chatbot. - The demo we just watched → agent. - Siri setting a timer → closer to an agent (it takes an action), though older Siri wasn't an LLM at all. Why it matters: more power = more risk. A chatbot can be wrong in words. An agent can be wrong in ACTIONS (delete a file, send an email). That's why agents ask permission, and why we check their work.

05

Question it: AI ethics

Who it helps. Who it hurts. Who checks.

"You now know more about how AI works than most adults. That's exactly why you get a say in how it's used. Five big issues: bias, truth, fakes, privacy, and the big questions about ownership, honesty, jobs and energy. Every week has an AI Checkpoint on one of these."

Ethics 1 · Bias

It learned from us. Biases too.

1

Unfair examples, unfair patterns

The dials copy whatever is in the data. They can't tell fair from unfair.

2

It has happened

Amazon scrapped a hiring AI that marked down résumés with the word “women's.”

3

Who gets missed?

A 2018 study found face AIs far less accurate for darker-skinned women.

Always ask: who is this unfair to?

~2 min. The tablet is a simulation of the Amazon case: same skills, but the résumé that mentions a women's club scores lower, because the AI learned from ten years of past hires who were mostly men. Click 2: reported by Reuters in 2018. Amazon said the tool was never used on its own to make hiring decisions, and it was scrapped. The point: nobody programmed "prefer men". The pattern was in the examples. Click 3: the "Gender Shades" study (Joy Buolamwini & Timnit Gebru, MIT, 2018). Commercial face tools guessing gender were wrong up to 34.7% of the time for darker-skinned women vs. 0.8% for lighter-skinned men. Why: the training photos had far fewer darker-skinned faces. Discussion (30 sec): "What could go wrong if an AI like this decided who gets into a school? Who gets a loan?" Building tip for later weeks: test your project with different kinds of users, not just people like you.

Ethics 2 · Truth  ·  with your partner · 3 minutes

Ask your AI these. Then check.

Q1What time does the Burch Library close on Saturdays?
Q2Who is the mayor of Collierville right now?
Q3What's the newest restaurant on the Town Square?

Score each:

✓ right

✗ wrong

? made up / can't tell

Check against: the official website · a map app · a librarian
~3 min. Pairs use ChatGPT, Gemini, or whatever AI they're allowed to use. Timer: 3 minutes. LEADERS: look up the real answers the day before from official sources, and swap in fresher questions if these become too easy. Click 2 (Score each): the three cards top-right flip to ✗ ? ✓. They show the three possible scores, not the real answers. If an AI searched the web it may get these right. Then score its SOURCES: open one. Does the page say that? Debrief: hands up, who got at least one ✗ or ? Ask a pair to read out the most confident wrong answer.

Why does that happen?

Fluent is not the same as true.

Sounds certain. Nobody checked.

It's predicting words,not looking things up (unless it searches).

Its knowledge has a cutoff,so local + recent facts are weak.

Coaching rewarded sounding sure,so it rarely says “I don't know.”

So you are the fact-checker. Always.
~1.5 min. The phone types out an example of a confident answer (we made it up for the slide; it's the kind of thing AIs say). Click: UNVERIFIED stamp. This has a name: HALLUCINATION. Connect each reason to what we learned: 1. Step 4–5: it picks likely-sounding tokens. A made-up time "sounds like" a library's hours. 2. Training vs. using: training froze its knowledge at a cutoff date. 3. Coaching (human ratings): people tend to rate confident answers higher, so it learned confidence. This is also why AI-written code can look perfect and still be broken.

Ethics 3 · Deepfakes

Seeing isn't believing.

1

Fake photos, video and voices

A few seconds of someone's voice can be enough to clone it.

2

Check before you share

Who posted it first? Is a trusted news site reporting it? Ask for the source.

3

Make a family code word

If “Mom” calls panicking and asks for money, ask for the word.

Too shocking? Check before you share.

~2 min. The laptop shows two scenes we made up for the slide: a viral "shark on Main Street" post getting fact-checked, and a phone call from a cloned voice. Click 1: image generators (slide 19!) and voice models make fakes cheap. Voice-clone scams are real: a short clip from a video you posted can be enough. Click 2: the checks. Find the ORIGINAL poster (new account? no name?). Search the claim: are real news outlets reporting it? Reverse image search (Google Lens) to see where the photo first appeared. Look for oddities, but don't rely on spotting glitches; good fakes don't have any. Click 3: agree on a family code word tonight. It costs nothing and beats any detector. Also: making a deepfake of a real person (especially a classmate) can be bullying, and in many places it's illegal.

Ethics 4 · Privacy  ·  not in prompts, not on your site

Never share these online.

✗Your full name
✗Your school
✗Your address
✗Phone numbers
✗Photos of people
✗Passwords or keys

Chats can be saved and used to train AI. And always: an adult checks your site before you share it.

~1.5 min. "A chat feels private. It isn't a diary." - What you type is stored on the company's servers. - Depending on the app and your settings, it can be read by reviewers and used to train future models. (Show where the "improve the model for everyone" / training setting lives in one app.) - Anything on your website is public to the whole planet. Rule of thumb: if you wouldn't post it publicly, don't put it in a prompt. Use a nickname or first name only on your site. No sign-up forms, no collecting other people's info. If you're not sure, ask a leader.

Ethics 5 · The big questions

Who owns it? Who pays?

OWNERSHIP

Whose work did it learn from?

Artists' and writers' work, often without asking. Lawsuits are ongoing. In the U.S., purely AI-made work can't be copyrighted.

HONESTY

When is it cheating?

Using AI isn't cheating when it's allowed and you say so. Passing off AI work as your own is.

JOBS

What happens to work?

AI changes the tasks inside many jobs. People who can direct, check and fix AI's work stay valuable.

ENERGY

What does it cost the planet?

Data centers used about 1.5% of the world's electricity in 2024, set to double by 2030. One prompt is tiny; billions add up.

~2 min. One card per click. These don't have settled answers; that's the point. Ask for one opinion per card. OWNERSHIP: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023; Getty Images sued Stability AI. Courts are still deciding whether training on copyrighted work is "fair use". The U.S. Copyright Office says work needs real human authorship to be copyrighted, so a prompt alone usually isn't enough. HONESTY: our rule all six weeks: AI help is fine, hiding it isn't. Your README (week 5) says what AI did and what you did. JOBS: ask "what part of your dream job would you NOT want an AI to do? Why?" ENERGY: International Energy Agency, Energy and AI report (2025): about 415 TWh in 2024, around 945 TWh projected for 2030. Google reported a typical Gemini text prompt uses about 0.24 watt-hours (roughly 9 seconds of TV). Small each; it's the scale, plus training giant models, that adds up. Cooling also uses water.

06

Build with it.

Start a live page today. Finish it at home.

Energy up. Laptops open. "Four minutes of how-to, then you build for twenty."

Not all AI tools are the same

Pick the right tool.

1

Learning modes · start here

ChatGPT Study mode, Gemini Guided Learning, CS50 Duck, Khanmigo. They coach, not just answer.

2

Chat assistants

ChatGPT (13+, with a parent's OK under 18) and Gemini teen accounts. Claude is 18+.

3

Code helpers

GitHub Copilot lives inside your code editor. Free tier, plus free Pro for verified students.

4

App builders

Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit build whole apps. Mostly 18+ or need a parent, so leaders demo.

~1.5 min. Check each tool's age rules before the session; they change often. 1 LEARNING MODES (guardrailed): these are built to guide you with questions and hints instead of handing over the answer. ChatGPT Study mode and Gemini Guided Learning are switches inside the normal apps. CS50 Duck (cs50.ai) is Harvard CS50's coding tutor, designed not to just give you the solution. Khanmigo (Khan Academy) works this way too; it's free through some schools, otherwise paid. 2 CHAT ASSISTANTS: great for explaining and brainstorming. Turn on the learning mode for code. 3 CODE HELPERS: autocomplete and chat inside VS Code. GitHub Education gives verified students Copilot Pro free. 4 APP BUILDERS: type a description, get an entire app. Amazing, but you learn the least, and most require 18+ or parent permission (Lovable: 18 or parent's OK; Replit's current terms: adults). Leaders can demo them. TODAY: a chat assistant in tutor mode (next slide) + GitHub.

Prompting well

Vague in. Vague out.

VAGUE

make me a website

→ it guesses everything.

CLEAR · THIS IS TUTOR MODE · COPY IT

GOALHelp me build one index.html page that says “Hi, I'm [first name].”
DETAILSMy favorite color as the background. One button that does something fun.
LIMITSI'm a beginner. Explain your plan in 3 bullets first. Short code, a comment above each part.
CHECKAfter the code, ask me one question to check I understand it.
~1.5 min. Read the vague prompt. "What will it make?" Nobody knows, and neither does the AI. Remember the machine: it predicts from what's on the page. The more you put on the page, the less it guesses. Click: the clear version, which is also our tutor-mode prompt. GOAL (what), DETAILS (how it should look/act), LIMITS (rules, including "explain first" and "short code"), CHECK (makes it test YOU). Put this text on the handout / shared link so everyone can copy it. The laptop shows what a good answer looks like: a plan, short commented code, then a question. Two more habits: iterate one change at a time ("now make the button bigger"), and if it breaks, paste the error message plus what you expected to happen.

How we build here  ·  plan → build small → test → explain

The 4 habits.

1

Explain-back

No AI code goes in your project until you can explain it out loud.

2

Tutor mode

Hints and a plan first. Full code second.

3

Pair up

Side by side, each on your own site. Review each other's work. Leaders never grab your keyboard.

4

Prompt journal

Write down what you asked, what came back, what broke.

~1 min. One click per habit, and each brings in its object: a mic (explain it out loud), a bulb (hints first), two cursors (pair up: partners sit together, each building their own site, and check each other), a notebook (journal). These are the rules every week, not just today. The workflow in the kicker: plan what you want, ask for a SMALL piece, test it in the browser, explain it back. Why? Research on beginners using AI to code: the ones who let AI do everything end up unable to fix or change their own project. The ones who use it like a tutor get better. Hand out the printed habits card.

~20 min, guided. Walk through all five together, one click at a time, with the room following along. The browser on the right acts out each step as you click. Both leaders circulate. Hands off the keyboard: point, don't type. Goal for today: EVERYONE LIVE. Do steps 1, 2, 4, 5 in the room with a one-line placeholder for step 3:

Hi, I'm [first name]

. That way Build Lab 1 (repo, commit, Pages) happens with leaders in the room. At home, step 3 for real: the tutor-mode prompt builds the actual page, which replaces the placeholder. No GitHub account / no permission form? They pair with someone and watch today.

YOUR SITE LIVES HERE

https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/my-first-site

Takes 1–2 minutes after step 5. Refresh.

Live today. The real page comes at home.

Not loading? Re-check Settings → Pages.

For whoever gets live today: have them type their URL into the shared doc / form for the "wall of URLs" at the start of Session 2. "Shipped" means three things by demo day: (1) a public URL that loads on a phone, (2) at least one interactive thing that works, (3) a README saying what the AI did and what you did. The globe: once it's live, anyone on Earth with the link can open it. That's why the privacy rules matter.
